planting.note: Set out divisions or container plants in spring in humus-rich, evenly moist soil; this century-old Dutch selection flowers best where summers are not excessively hot.

directions: One of the oldest named Geum cultivars still in commerce, Prinses Juliana carries loosely semi-double flowers in warm burnt-orange over mounds of hairy, deeply cut basal foliage. It blooms heavily in late spring and will often repeat lightly into summer if deadheaded. Give it steady moisture and a cool root zone, since it fades quickly in hot, dry spells. Divide every three years or so to keep clumps vigorous and free-flowering.

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in fertile, well-drained soil; this long-grown German hybrid tolerates more heat than many Geum cultivars.

directions: Werner Arends is a classic Geum hybrid grown for its coppery orange-red single flowers held above clumps of scalloped, semi-evergreen foliage. It flowers over a long stretch from late spring into summer and attracts bees readily. Grown in average garden soil with reliable drainage, it is sturdier and less floppy than many showier double-flowered Geum cultivars. Lift and divide congested clumps every two to three years to maintain bloom quality.

planting.note: Set out container-grown plants in spring in fertile, consistently moist but well-drained soil; a Terra Nova Nurseries introduction bred for larger flowers on a compact frame.

directions: Scarlet Tempest produces unusually large, semi-double scarlet-red flowers on wiry stems that stand well above a tidy mound of dark green foliage. Repeat bloom is strong from late spring through midsummer, especially if spent flower stems are trimmed back promptly. It performs best with consistent moisture and a bit of afternoon shade in hotter climates. Compact habit makes it useful toward the front of a mixed perennial border.

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring in fertile, well-drained soil amended with compost; a Terra Nova Nurseries hybrid from their cocktail-themed Geum breeding line.

directions: Mai Tai bears semi-double flowers that open peachy-apricot and age to soft tangerine, creating a two-tone effect across each cluster of blooms. The compact mound of lobed foliage stays tidy through the season, and flowering continues intermittently from late spring into summer with light grooming. It is best sited where soil stays evenly moist but never waterlogged. Use it in mixed borders or containers where its warm color can be appreciated up close.

planting.note: Install rooted cuttings or container stock in spring or fall into well-drained soil; this prostrate selection of the California native shrub is grown strictly as a groundcover, never as an upright hedge.

directions: Pigeon Point is a low, spreading selection of coyote brush that forms a dense, mounding mat of small gray-green leaves, useful for erosion control on slopes and as a tough, low-maintenance groundcover. Once established it needs little to no supplemental irrigation and tolerates coastal wind, salt spray, and poor soils. Only the female clone is typically propagated for landscape use, which avoids the messy white seed fluff produced by male plants. Occasional shearing in late winter keeps growth dense and prevents woody, leggy stems.
sources: University of California Marin Master Gardeners

planting.note: Install rooted cuttings or container stock in spring or fall into well-drained soil; a compact dwarf form of the California native shrub used as a tidy, low groundcover.

directions: Twin Peaks forms a dense, finely textured mat of small gray-green foliage that stays lower and more compact than most other coyote brush groundcover selections. It is widely planted along freeway margins and slopes in coastal California for its drought tolerance and resistance to foot traffic once established. Give it full sun and sharply drained soil, and avoid summer irrigation once roots are established to prevent fungal problems. Light shearing after the first year or two encourages dense branching and a uniform carpet effect.

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring after frost danger passes into lean, sharply drained soil; like other Texas sage cultivars it rots quickly in heavy or constantly damp ground.

directions: Silverado is grown for its densely felted, intensely silvery foliage that outshines the straight species even when not in bloom. Lavender-purple flowers appear in flushes after summer humidity rises, often following rain events rather than on a fixed schedule. It thrives in hot, dry, alkaline soils and declines quickly if overwatered or planted in heavy clay. Avoid hard pruning into formal shapes, since this spoils the natural rounded form and reduces flowering.
